claim: When you enable replication, Amazon EFS automatically and transparently replicates the data and metadata of the source file system to a destination file system.
question: What does EFS replication copy to the destination file system?

values.display: data and metadata on the source file system

evidence.quote: When you enable replication on an EFS file system, Amazon EFS automatically and transparently replicates the data and metadata on the source file system to a destination file system.

claim: EFS Replication copies your file system data into a new or existing file system in the Region of your choice, transferring only incremental changes.
question: Where does EFS Replication copy a file system, and how are changes sent?

evidence.quote: Amazon EFS Replication copies your file system data into a new or existing file system in the Region of your choice. It keeps the two file systems synchronized by automatically transferring only incremental changes without requiring additional infrastructure or a custom process.

claim: EFS replication is continual and designed to provide a recovery point objective (RPO) and a recovery time objective (RTO) of minutes.
question: What recovery point and recovery time objectives does EFS replication target?

evidence.quote: Replication is continual and designed to provide a recovery point objective (RPO) and a recovery time objective (RTO) of minutes.

claim: After the initial replication finishes, Amazon EFS maintains a recovery point objective (RPO) of 15 minutes for most file systems.
question: What RPO does EFS replication maintain after the initial sync?

evidence.quote: After the initial replication is finished, Amazon EFS maintains a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of 15 minutes for most file systems.

claim: If the source file system has files that change very frequently and has either more than 100 million files or files larger than 100 GB, replication may take longer than 15 minutes.
question: When can EFS replication take longer than 15 minutes?

evidence.quote: However, if the source file system has files that change very frequently and has either more than 100 million files or files that are larger than 100 GB, replication may take longer than 15 minutes.

claim: Replicated data is accessible in the destination file system only after the initial sync completes, and how long that takes depends on the size of the source and the number of files.
question: When is replicated data available in the destination EFS file system?

values.display: only after the initial sync completes
size of the source file system

evidence.quote: Replicated data is accessible in the destination file system only after the initial sync completes. The amount of time that the initial sync takes to finish depends on factors such as the size of the source file system and the number of files in it.

claim: EFS replication is not point-in-time consistent: changes are transferred based on the last synced time, and changes made after that time may not be replicated.
question: Is an EFS replica point-in-time consistent?

evidence.quote: Changes made to the source file system are not transferred to the destination file system in a point-in-time consistent manner.
No. EFS Replication doesn't provide point-in-time consistent replication.

claim: The destination file system of EFS replication is read-only while replication is enabled, and applications can use it in read-only mode for low-latency cross-Region access.
question: Can you write to the replica of an EFS file system while replication is on?

values.display: use the replica file system in read-only mode

evidence.quote: Amazon EFS automatically creates a new file system and copies the data and metadata on the source file system to a new read-only destination file system in the AWS Region that you choose.
While EFS Replication is enabled, your applications can use the replica file system in read-only mode for low network latency cross-Region access.

claim: You can use EFS Replication to replicate your file system to a Region or Availability Zone of your choice, without managing additional infrastructure or custom processes.

without having to manage additional infrastructure

claim: To fail over to the replica file system you delete its replication configuration; after the configuration is deleted the replica becomes writeable and you can use it in your application workflow.
question: How do you fail over to an EFS replica?

evidence.quote: In the event of a disaster or when performing game day exercises, you can fail over to your replica file system by deleting its replication configuration. After the replication configuration is deleted, the replica becomes writeable and you can start using it in your application workflow.

claim: During failback you can choose to discard the changes made to the replica during failover, or preserve them by copying them back to the primary file system.
question: What choices do you have when failing back to the primary EFS file system?

values.display: discard the changes made to your replica
preserve them by copying them back

evidence.quote: During the failback process, you can choose to discard the changes made to your replica file system or preserve them by copying them back to your primary.

claim: Deleting a replication configuration and changing the destination file system to be writeable can take several minutes, and you can delete the configuration from either the source or the destination file system.

either the source or the destination

claim: A file system can be part of only one replication configuration, and a destination file system cannot be the source of another replication configuration.

cannot use a destination file system
